summary:
A stretch `a … b` sums to `target` exactly when `prefix[b + 1] − prefix[a] = target`, i.e. when an earlier
prefix sum equals `currentPrefix − target`. Walk once, keep a hash map counting the prefix sums seen so far,
and add the count of `prefix − target` at every step. O(n).

question.md:
Count the non-empty runs of consecutive elements whose sum is exactly `target`.

- **Counts runs by position:** two different runs with the same values both count. In `[0, 0]` with
  target 0 there are 3 runs: each single 0 and the pair.
- **Negative numbers are allowed**, so a run's sum can go up and down. That rules out the sliding-window
  trick (which needs sums that only grow as the window grows).
- **Size:** up to 10⁵ elements; the count can reach about 5 × 10⁹ (all-zero input, target 0), so return
  it as a 64-bit integer.

think.md: Take `nums = [1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 3]` with target 3. Write down the prefix sums (the sum of the first k elements):

think.caption: Runs summing to 3 are pairs of prefix sums that differ by 3.

think.md:
The run from index a to index b sums to `prefix[b + 1] − prefix[a]`. So when you're at the end of a run
with running sum `p`, the runs ending here that hit the target are exactly the earlier prefixes equal to
`p − 3`, however many of them there are.

So keep a **count of every prefix sum seen so far** (starting with the empty prefix, 0, seen once). At
each element: add `count[p − target]` to the answer, then record `p`. Here that totals 5.

approaches.title: Every start, running sum

idea.md: For each start i, extend j with a running sum; count every time it equals the target. (Re-adding each run from scratch would be O(n³); carrying the sum while extending saves a factor of n.)

build: For each j ≥ i: `s += nums[j]`; if `s == target`, count it.

lines.text: Grow the run one element at a time, carrying its sum (within ±10⁸, fine for `int`).

walk.title: Try every start; extend to every end with a running sum; count the sums equal to the target.

limits.md: Each run's sum is a difference of two prefix sums. Instead of pairing every start with every end, look up how many earlier prefixes complete the target.

approaches.title: Prefix sums with a hash map of counts

idea.md: Keep `seen[s]`, how many prefixes so far had sum s, starting with `seen[0] = 1`. For each element: update the running prefix `p`, add `seen[p − target]` to the answer, then do `seen[p] += 1`.

build: For each x: `p += x`; `count += seen[p − target]`; `seen[p] += 1`.

lines.text: C has no hash map: `slotFor` hashes a prefix sum to a starting slot and walks forward to its entry or to the empty slot where it would go.
The empty prefix (before any element) has sum 0 and has been seen once; that lets runs starting at index 0 be counted.

notes.c: The table holds up to n + 1 distinct prefix sums, so it's sized at least twice that.

lines.text: Running prefix sum, including the current element (within ±10⁸).
Every earlier prefix equal to `prefix − target` starts a run that ends here and sums to the target.
Only now add the current prefix, so a run can't be empty (it would need `target = 0` with start = end).

complexity.md: **Time O(n)** on average. **Space O(n)** for up to n + 1 distinct prefix sums.

steps.text: The empty prefix (sum 0) has been seen once.
Index 0: prefix 1; need earlier prefix 1 − 3 = -2, seen 0 times → count 0. Then record prefix 1.
Index 1: prefix 3; need earlier prefix 3 − 3 = 0, seen 1 time → count 1. Then record prefix 3.
Index 2: prefix 4; need earlier prefix 4 − 3 = 1, seen 1 time → count 2. Then record prefix 4.
Index 3: prefix 6; need earlier prefix 6 − 3 = 3, seen 1 time → count 3. Then record prefix 6.
Index 4: prefix 7; need earlier prefix 7 − 3 = 4, seen 1 time → count 4. Then record prefix 7.
Index 5: prefix 10; need earlier prefix 10 − 3 = 7, seen 1 time → count 5. Then record prefix 10.

walk.title: A stretch ending at i sums to 3 when some earlier prefix equals prefix − 3. Count earlier prefixes in a hash map.

takeaways.md:
- **Count subarrays with sum = k:** walk with a running prefix sum and a hash map of how often each prefix
  occurred; add `count[prefix − k]` each step. Start with `count[0] = 1`.
- Look up before recording, so empty subarrays aren't counted.
- With negatives present, sliding windows don't work; prefix sums do.
